# Migrating to tabular-center

Every library below lets you *list* transitions. tabular-center asks for a
*grid*: one cell for every state and every action, each decided explicitly.
That is the whole migration, and it is also the whole gain -- the cells a
listing never mentions are exactly the ones a grid will not let you forget.
Add a state or an action and the build breaks until every new cell has an
answer; add an effect and every handler breaks until it performs it.

The "before" sketches are written against each library's documented API to
show the shape of the code you have now. They are not compiled here; check
them against the version you use. The "after" code is included from this
repository's examples, which CI builds and runs.

## The concepts, mapped

| You have | You write |
|---|---|
| a state | a row |
| an event / action | a column |
| a transition to a fixed state, maybe with a side effect | `GO(Target, Effect...)` -- no code |
| a transition whose target is computed, or guarded | `HANDLE` -- one method, arguments already narrowed |
| an event that does nothing in this state (often: silently unlisted) | `IGNORE`, written down |
| an event that must never arrive in this state | `UNREACHABLE` -- a trap, counted by coverage |
| a target-less / internal transition with a side effect | `EMIT(Effect...)` |
| side-effect listeners, `onTransition`, actions | an effects enum, and one `perform` member per effect |
| a composite / nested state | `DELEGATE(child)` -- a child machine, composed, not nested |

## What has no equivalent

Said up front, because each is a real feature of the libraries below:

- **Hierarchy, parallel regions, history states.** tabular-center composes
  flat machines with `DELEGATE` rather than nesting states. A statechart with
  orthogonal regions becomes two machines side by side.
- **Entry and exit actions.** Put the work in the effects of the transitions
  that enter or leave the state -- which makes it visible in the grid, at the
  cost of repeating it on each such transition.
- **Machines built at runtime.** The matrix is a declaration the compiler
  checks; there is no builder to call in a loop.
- **Persistence and undo.** State is a value you own: store it, restore it,
  keep the previous one if you need to go back.

## From Tinder StateMachine (Kotlin)

A stopwatch -- `Idle` and `Running(since)`, `Start` and `Stop`, a `Beep` on
stopping -- in Tinder's DSL:

```kotlin
// Sketch against com.tinder.StateMachine's documented DSL; not compiled here.
val stopwatch = StateMachine.create<State, Event, SideEffect> {
    initialState(State.Idle)
    state<State.Idle> {
        on<Event.Start> { transitionTo(State.Running(clock.now())) }
    }
    state<State.Running> {
        on<Event.Stop> {
            lastElapsed = clock.now() - since
            transitionTo(State.Idle, SideEffect.Beep)
        }
    }
    onTransition {
        val valid = it as? StateMachine.Transition.Valid ?: return@onTransition
        if (valid.sideEffect == SideEffect.Beep) beeps++
    }
}
```

`Stop` while `Idle` and `Start` while `Running` appear nowhere: they come back
as `Transition.Invalid` at runtime, and nothing says whether that was meant.
The same machine here -- the two unlisted pairs are `IGNORE`, on the page:

```kotlin
@Machine(
    states = [S.Idle::class, S.Running::class],
    actions = [A.Start::class, A.Stop::class],
    effects = [F.Beep::class],
    initial = S.Idle::class,
)
//                         Start                    Stop
@Row(S.Idle::class,      [CellSpec(Kind.HANDLE),  CellSpec(Kind.IGNORE)])
@Row(S.Running::class,   [CellSpec(Kind.IGNORE),  CellSpec(Kind.HANDLE)])
internal interface StopwatchSpec {
    /**
     * `Clock.` is the whole fixture, as `suspend` is Gate's.
     *
     * The generator copies the receiver onto every member it emits, the same
     * way it copies modifiers: it does not know what a `Clock` is and does not
     * need to. `internal` on the interface above is the other half -- the
     * generated surface takes its visibility from here.
     */
    fun Clock.handle(ctx: Ctx, state: S, action: A): Step<S, F>
}
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-kotlin/examples/06-generated/src/Stopwatch.tb.kt`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-kotlin/examples/06-generated/src/Stopwatch.tb.kt).</sub>

KSP turns the two `HANDLE` cells and the one effect into three members, each
receiving its state and action already narrowed -- `state.since` is a field,
not a cast:

```kotlin
internal class StopwatchImpl : Cells {
    override fun Clock.idleStart(ctx: Ctx, state: S.Idle, action: A.Start): Step<S, F> =
        Step.Go(S.Running(now()))

    override fun Clock.runningStop(ctx: Ctx, state: S.Running, action: A.Stop): Step<S, F> {
        ctx.lastElapsed = now() - state.since
        return Step.Go(S.Idle, listOf(F.Beep))
    }

    override fun Clock.beep(ctx: Ctx, effect: F.Beep): A? {
        ctx.beeps++
        return null
    }
}
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-kotlin/examples/06-generated/src/StopwatchImpl.kt`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-kotlin/examples/06-generated/src/StopwatchImpl.kt).</sub>

`onTransition`'s `as?` and `if` become `beep`, which the compiler requires.

## From KStateMachine (Kotlin)

```kotlin
// Sketch against KStateMachine's documented DSL; not compiled here.
val machine = createStateMachine(scope) {
    addInitialState(StopwatchState.Idle) {
        transition<Start> {
            targetState = StopwatchState.Running
            onTriggered { since = clock.now() }
        }
    }
    addState(StopwatchState.Running) {
        transition<Stop> {
            targetState = StopwatchState.Idle
            onTriggered {
                lastElapsed = clock.now() - since
                beeps++
            }
        }
    }
}
machine.processEvent(Start)
```

The declaration is the same as above: `transition<Start> { targetState = ... }`
with `onTriggered` work is a `HANDLE` cell; one with no work is `GO`; a
target-less one is a `HANDLE` that stays -- or `EMIT`, when its only work is
an effect. KStateMachine's states are instances, so
`since` lives outside them; here it is the payload of `Running`, and a cell
cannot see it from any other state. Its coroutine support maps to a `suspend`
prototype -- `suspend fun handle(...)` -- and `SuspendDriver`, with no
coroutine library needed by the runtime.

## From Spring Statemachine (Java or Kotlin)

```java
// Sketch against Spring Statemachine's documented configurer; not compiled here.
@Override
public void configure(StateMachineTransitionConfigurer<States, Events> transitions)
        throws Exception {
    transitions
        .withExternal().source(States.IDLE).target(States.RUNNING).event(Events.START)
            .action(ctx -> since = clock.now())
        .and()
        .withExternal().source(States.RUNNING).target(States.IDLE).event(Events.STOP)
            .action(ctx -> { lastElapsed = clock.now() - since; beeps++; });
}
```

Move to the Kotlin surface above: each `withExternal()` is a cell, an
`.action(...)` makes it `HANDLE`, a `.guard(...)` belongs inside that same
`HANDLE` as an `if`, and every `source`/`event` pair you did not configure
becomes a cell you decide. What does not come along is the container: there
is no bean, no `@EnableStateMachine`, no message channel. A machine is a
function from a state and an action to a step, and `Driver` or
`SuspendDriver` runs it.

## From TCA (Swift)

The Composable Architecture is not a state-machine library, but a reducer
that switches on its state and action is a state machine -- with a
`default:` that decides every pair nobody wrote down:

```swift
// Sketch against TCA 1.x's documented reducer; not compiled here.
@Reducer
struct Timer {
    @ObservableState
    enum State: Equatable { case idle, running(since: Int), done }
    enum Action { case start, tick(now: Int), cancel }

    var body: some ReducerOf<Self> {
        Reduce { state, action in
            switch (state, action) {
            case (.idle, .start):
                state = .running(since: 0)
                return .run { _ in await clock.start() }
            case let (.running(since), .tick(now)):
                guard now - since >= limit else { return .none }
                state = .done
                return .run { _ in await clock.stop() }
            case (.running, .cancel):
                state = .idle
                return .run { _ in await clock.stop() }
            case (.done, .start):
                state = .running(since: 0)
                return .run { _ in await clock.start() }
            default:
                return .none
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The same Timer as a matrix. The `default:` is gone; its five cases are `IGNORE`
cells you can see, and the two static transitions need no code at all:

```swift
extension Timer {
    static let TABLE = Table(
        machine: "Timer",
        states: ["Idle", "Running", "Done"],
        actions: ["Start", "Tick", "Cancel"],
        cells: [
            [.handle, .ignore, .ignore],
            [.ignore, .handle, .go(target: "Idle", effects: ["StopClock"])],
            [.go(target: "Running", effects: ["StartClock"]), .ignore, .ignore],
        ],
        initial: "Idle"
    )
}
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-swift/examples/Sources/Timer/Timer.tb.swift`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-swift/examples/Sources/Timer/Timer.tb.swift).</sub>

The two computed cells, and the effects that replace the `.run` closures:

```swift
    struct Impl: Cells {
        func idleStart(_ ctx: Ctx) -> Step<S, F> {
            .go(.running(since: 0), effects: [.startClock])
        }

        func runningTick(_ ctx: Ctx, _ state: Running, _ action: Tick) -> Step<S, F> {
            // No `if case`, no cast, no force-unwrap: the dispatcher matched.
            if action.now - state.since >= ctx.limit {
                return .go(.done, effects: [.stopClock(reason: .elapsed)])
            }
            // Handled, and staying put. Distinct from `.ignored`, which would
            // claim a tick is meaningless while running.
            return .stay(effects: [])
        }

        func startClock(_ ctx: Ctx) -> A? {
            ctx.log.append("start")
            return nil
        }

        func stopClock(_ ctx: Ctx, _ reason: Reason) -> A? {
            ctx.log.append("stop:\(reason)")
            return nil
        }
    }
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-swift/examples/Sources/Timer/Timer.swift`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-swift/examples/Sources/Timer/Timer.swift).</sub>

`@ObservableState` maps to `ObservableStore`, a `@MainActor` store SwiftUI can
observe. `TestStore`'s role is shared: exhaustive behaviour tests stay yours,
and `TabularCenterTesting`'s `.tbl` fixtures pin the matrix itself, one reviewable
line per row. See [Swift](swift) for what is available today and what waits
on the `@Machine` macro.
